title: A bird on a plum branch
translation: The Okamoto regent once told his falconer, Shimotsukeno no Takekatsu, to tie a pair of birds to a branch of red plum in full bloom and bring it to him. Takekatsu said: "I don't know how to tie a bird to blossoms, my lord. And I've never heard of putting two on one branch."

The regent asked the kitchen staff, and had other people asked too. Then he told Takekatsu: "All right. Tie it the way you think best and bring it." Takekatsu tied one bird to a plum branch with no blossoms on it and brought that.

He explained it to me himself. "You use a branch of brushwood or plum, either in bud or after the blossoms have fallen. Five-needle pine works too. The branch is seven feet long, or six, with the end cut at a slant, and the bird goes in the middle. There's one branch you tie it to and one it stands on. Tie it in two places with unsplit vine. Trim the ends of the vine to the length of a wing feather and bend them like an ox's horns.

"You take it on the morning of the first snow. You carry the branch on your shoulder and come in through the middle gate with proper dignity. You step along the paving stones under the eaves, so you leave no tracks in the snow, pull out a few of the small feathers from the wings and scatter them, and lean the branch against the railing of the hall. If they give you a reward, you put it over your shoulder, bow, and leave. First snow or not, if it isn't deep enough to cover the toes of your shoes, you don't go. You scatter the feathers because a hawk grabs a bird by the soft part of its back. It shows that His Lordship's hawk caught it."

So why no birds on blossoms? I wonder what the reason was. In the Tales of Ise, a man ties a pheasant to an artificial plum branch in late autumn, with the words "the flowers I break for you know no season". Maybe artificial blossoms are all right.

literal: The Okamoto regent ordered his falconer, Shimotsukeno no Takekatsu, to attach a pair of birds to a branch of red plum in full bloom and to present it attached to this branch, and (Takekatsu) said, 'I do not know the technique of attaching birds to blossoms, and I do not know of attaching two to one branch either', so

(the regent) asked the kitchen staff and had people asked, and again ordered Takekatsu, 'In that case, attach it in the way you think and present it', and he attached one to a plum branch with no blossoms and presented it.
What Takekatsu told me was: 'We attach it to a branch of brushwood or a branch of plum, budding or with (the blossoms) fallen.
We also attach it to a five-needle pine and the like.
The length of the branch is seven feet or six feet, cut with a turned blade at five bu; we attach the bird at the middle of the branch.
There is a branch to attach it to and a branch for it to stand on.
One should attach it in two places with unsplit shijira vine.
The tips of the vine one should cut to compare with the length of the hiuchi feather, and bend them like the horns of an ox.
On the morning of the first snow, one puts the branch on one's shoulder and comes in through the middle gate with dignified bearing.
Going along the stones of the great paved edge, not leaving tracks in the snow, one plucks and scatters a few of the covert feathers, and leans it against the railing of the two-ridged hall.
If a reward is given, one puts it on one's shoulder, bows, and withdraws.
Even if it is the first snow, one does not go in snow so shallow that it does not hide the tips of the shoes.
Scattering the covert feathers: since a hawk seizes (a bird) at the weak loins, it must be to show that the lord's hawk caught it', he said.
That one does not attach birds to blossoms: what reason might there have been?
That around the ninth month someone attached a pheasant to an artificial plum branch and said 'The flowers I break for you know no season' appears in the Tales of Ise.
Are artificial flowers perhaps no problem?

notes.text: Usually identified as Konoe Iehira (1282–1324), who served as regent ({関白|くわんぱく}). Okamoto is the name by which he was known.
Birds caught by hawks were given as presents tied to a branch. Falconry was a court art with its own secret rules, handed down in particular families, and how to tie the bird was one of them.

The Shimotsukeno were a family of guards who served the regents' houses for generations, and falconry was part of their trade. Takekatsu's polite {候|さうら}ふ and {存|ぞん}ず are the speech of a servant to his lord, but what he says is a refusal: it isn't done.
{膳部|かしはで}: the kitchen staff. They prepared the birds for the table, which is presumably why the regent asked them.
き: past that Kenkō experienced himself. He heard the rules from Takekatsu in person, and he writes them down as Takekatsu said them, as a list.
{五分|ごぶ}: about 1.5 cm. かへし{刀|かたな} is usually explained as a cut made from one side and then the other, leaving a slanted end; the details are not certain. The translation keeps only the slant.

Falconry terms for feathers: {雨覆|あまおほ}ひ are the small feathers that cover the base of the long wing feathers, and {火|ひ}うち{羽|ば} is usually explained as a feather near the bend of the wing. The translation simplifies both.

A hall with a double roof ridge in a noble's mansion, probably the one where visitors were received. {禄|ろく}, the reward, was usually a robe or a length of cloth, which the receiver put over his shoulder to leave.

notes.quote: 君がためにと折る花は時しもわかぬ
notes.text: From the Tales of Ise (episode 98): a man presents a pheasant on an artificial plum branch to the Chancellor in the ninth month, with the poem わが{頼|たの}む{君|きみ}がためにと{折|を}る{花|はな}は{時|とき}しもわかぬものにぞありける, 'the flowers I break for you, my lord, know no season'. Kenkō quotes only the middle.

notes.quote: いかなる故にかありけむ
notes.text: か … けむ: a guess about the past, 'what reason might there have been?' The section closes with another question, にや ('perhaps'), with the rest (あらむ) left out. Kenkō leaves both open.
